task: Chemistry internal assessment (scientific investigation): How does temperature affect the rate of the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, and what activation energy does this give?
text:
Research question: How does temperature (293 K to 333 K) affect the rate of reaction between 0.040 mol dm^-3 sodium thiosulfate and 1.0 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid, measured as 1/time for the sulfur precipitate to hide a printed cross, and what activation energy does this give?

Background: Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + SO2(g) + S(s) + H2O(l). The sulfur makes the mixture opaque, so rate is proportional to 1/t, where t is the time for a fixed amount to form. Only collisions with at least the activation energy Ea succeed, and that fraction rises steeply with temperature. From the Arrhenius equation, ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT); with identical concentrations in every run 1/t is proportional to k, so ln(1/t) against 1/T should be a straight line of gradient -Ea/R.

Variables: Independent: temperature, 20 to 60 °C in 10 °C steps, set by a thermostatic water bath (digital thermometer, ± 0.5 °C). Dependent: time for the cross to disappear. Controlled: 50.0 cm^3 ± 0.1 cm^3 thiosulfate and 5.0 cm^3 ± 0.05 cm^3 acid from the same stock bottles, since rate depends on concentration; the same 100 cm^3 flask and printed cross, so the amount of sulfur needed to hide it is constant; the same observer and lighting.

Method: Both solutions were warmed separately in the bath to within 0.5 °C of the target. The acid was poured into the thiosulfate, the stopwatch started, and the flask swirled once and placed on the cross. Temperature was read at the start and end and averaged; three trials per temperature. A pilot run at 70 °C was dropped because 5 s was too short to time reliably. Safety: sulfur dioxide is toxic and can trigger asthma, so I used small volumes beside an open window and neutralised finished mixtures in sodium carbonate solution. Goggles were worn.

Raw data (time for cross to disappear, three trials):
293 K: 96.8 s, 98.3 s, 97.1 s
303 K: 50.6 s, 51.9 s, 51.1 s
313 K: 26.5 s, 27.4 s, 26.8 s
323 K: 14.8 s, 15.5 s, 15.0 s
333 K: 8.7 s, 9.3 s, 9.0 s
Observation: the mixture turned pale yellow, then opaque; at 333 K the flask cooled by about 2 °C during the run.

Processing: Uncertainty in each mean is half the range (far larger than stopwatch precision). Example, 293 K: mean = (96.8 + 98.3 + 97.1)/3 = 97.4 s; uncertainty = (98.3 - 96.8)/2 = ± 0.8 s. ln(1/97.4) = -4.579, with absolute uncertainty equal to the fractional uncertainty in t, ± 0.008. Error bars in 1/T were negligible.
293 K: 97.4 s ± 0.8 s, ln(1/t) = -4.579 ± 0.008
303 K: 51.2 s ± 0.7 s, ln(1/t) = -3.936 ± 0.013
313 K: 26.9 s ± 0.5 s, ln(1/t) = -3.292 ± 0.017
323 K: 15.1 s ± 0.4 s, ln(1/t) = -2.715 ± 0.023
333 K: 9.0 s ± 0.3 s, ln(1/t) = -2.197 ± 0.033
The graph of ln(1/t) against 1/T is linear (R^2 = 0.999) with best-fit gradient -5840 K; maximum and minimum gradient lines through the error bars give -6060 K and -5570 K. Ea = 5840 x 8.314 = 48 600 J mol^-1, uncertainty = (6060 - 5570)/2 x 8.314 = ± 2000 J mol^-1, so Ea = 49 ± 2 kJ mol^-1.

Conclusion: Raising the temperature from 293 K to 333 K increased the rate (1/t) by a factor of 10.8, roughly doubling every 10 K. The linear Arrhenius plot, with every error bar touching the line, shows the rate depends exponentially on -1/T as predicted: a small temperature rise greatly increases the fraction of particles with energy above Ea. My Ea of 49 ± 2 kJ mol^-1 lies inside the 47 to 53 kJ mol^-1 range quoted in two undergraduate laboratory manuals I consulted, so it agrees with accepted values within my uncertainty.

Evaluation: Random error was small (0.8 to 3.3 %). The main weakness is systematic: at 323 K and 333 K the flask cooled on the bench, and my reaction time (about 0.5 s) is 6 % of a 9 s run but 0.5 % of a 97 s run. Both make high-temperature times too long, flattening the gradient, so Ea is probably underestimated; the 333 K point does sit slightly below the line. Judging the end point by eye is subjective, but with one observer it shifts every time similarly, so it affects the intercept more than the gradient and matters less. Also, 1/t is an average rate, not the initial rate. Improvements: keep the flask in a glass-sided water bath and replace the cross with a light sensor and data logger stopping at a fixed transmission, removing both cooling and reaction-time error; and extend the range down to 5 °C with an ice bath, where long times make timing errors negligible.

task: Chemistry internal assessment (scientific investigation): How does temperature affect the rate of the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, and what activation energy does this give?
text:
Research question: How does temperature affect the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid?

Introduction: When sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid, sulfur is made and the solution goes cloudy. According to collision theory, at a higher temperature the particles move faster and collide more often, so the reaction should be faster. My hypothesis is that as the temperature increases the time taken will decrease.

Variables: Independent variable: temperature (20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C). Dependent variable: time for the cross to disappear. Controlled variables: volume of sodium thiosulfate, volume of acid, concentration, same flask.

Method: I measured 50 cm^3 of sodium thiosulfate into a conical flask and heated it on a hot plate to the temperature needed. Then I added 5 cm^3 of hydrochloric acid, started the stopwatch (± 0.01 s) and put the flask on a piece of paper with a cross on it. I stopped timing when I could not see the cross. I repeated this three times for each temperature. I wore goggles.

Results (mean time of three trials, the trials were within about 1.5 s of each other):
20 °C: 97.4 s
30 °C: 51.2 s
40 °C: 26.9 s
50 °C: 15.1 s
60 °C: 9.0 s
I calculated rate = 1/time. For 20 °C: 1/97.4 = 0.0103 s^-1. For 60 °C: 1/9.0 = 0.111 s^-1. I plotted a graph of rate against temperature and it is a curve going upwards.

Conclusion: The graph shows that as temperature increases the rate of reaction increases, so my hypothesis was correct. The rate at 60 °C was about ten times the rate at 20 °C. The relationship is not a straight line, the rate goes up more and more quickly. This agrees with collision theory because the particles have more energy and collide more often, and more of them have the activation energy.

Evaluation: My results were quite reliable because I did three trials and they were close together. One weakness is that it was hard to decide exactly when the cross had disappeared, so the times could be a bit out. Another weakness is that the flask cooled down after I took it off the hot plate, especially at 60 °C. To improve I would use a water bath to keep the temperature constant and use a light sensor instead of my eyes.

task: Biology extended response: Over 20 years, the proportion of Staphylococcus aureus infections in a hospital that were resistant to methicillin rose from 2% to 40%. Explain how natural selection can account for this change and evaluate two strategies the hospital could use to slow the spread of resistance.
text:
Antibiotic resistance evolves by natural selection acting on heritable variation that already exists in the bacterial population. In S. aureus, random mutation, or genes acquired from other bacteria on plasmids by conjugation, means a small minority of cells carry a resistance allele; in MRSA this is the mecA gene, which codes for an altered penicillin-binding protein that methicillin cannot inhibit, so the cell wall is still built. The antibiotic does not cause the mutation. The 2% of resistant infections at the start shows the allele was already present at low frequency.

When patients are treated with methicillin, the drug acts as a selection pressure. Susceptible bacteria are killed, while resistant ones survive and reproduce by binary fission, passing the allele to all their offspring. Because bacteria can divide every 20 to 30 minutes and competition from susceptible cells has been removed, the allele frequency rises quickly within a patient. A hospital speeds this up: antibiotic use is heavy, so selection is strong and repeated, and patients with wounds and weak immune systems are close together, so resistant strains pass between them on hands and equipment. Over 20 years of repeated selection and transmission, a rise from 2% to 40% is what would be expected. That it has not reached 100% suggests resistance carries a cost when the drug is absent, or that susceptible strains keep arriving with new patients.

Strategy 1 is reducing and targeting antibiotic use, for example testing which drug a strain is sensitive to before prescribing. This weakens the selection pressure itself, so it addresses the cause, and it slows resistance to other drugs too. However, it delays treatment while tests are run, which is risky for very ill patients, and it cannot remove resistance genes that are already common. Strategy 2 is infection control: hand hygiene, screening on admission and isolating carriers. This does not change selection but cuts transmission, and it works immediately on strains that are already resistant. Its weakness is that it depends on constant staff compliance and on isolation rooms being available.

Overall neither is enough alone: stewardship slows the appearance of resistance while infection control limits its spread, so the hospital should combine them, with infection control likely to produce the quicker fall in the 40% figure.

task: Biology extended response: Over 20 years, the proportion of Staphylococcus aureus infections in a hospital that were resistant to methicillin rose from 2% to 40%. Explain how natural selection can account for this change and evaluate two strategies the hospital could use to slow the spread of resistance.
text:
Antibiotic resistance happens because of natural selection. In the population of bacteria there is variation, and some of the bacteria have a mutation that makes them resistant to methicillin. When the antibiotic is used, the bacteria that are not resistant die and the resistant ones survive. This is survival of the fittest. The resistant bacteria then reproduce and pass on the resistance gene to their offspring, so over time more and more of the bacteria are resistant. Bacteria reproduce very quickly so this can happen fast. This is why the hospital went from 2% to 40% resistant infections in 20 years. The more the antibiotic is used, the more the bacteria become immune to it.

To slow the spread the hospital could give out fewer antibiotics, so that there is less chance for resistant bacteria to be selected. Doctors should only prescribe them when they are really needed and patients should finish the course. The hospital could also make staff wash their hands and keep infected patients apart so the bacteria cannot spread to other people. Both of these would help to reduce resistance.

task: Mathematics exploration: What dimensions minimise the material used to make a 330 ml cylindrical drinks can, and why do real cans not have these dimensions?
text:
Introduction and rationale: While recycling at home I noticed that every 330 ml can, whatever the brand, has almost the same tall shape, yet a tin of tuna is short and wide. I expected manufacturers to choose the shape that uses least aluminium. My aim is to find the radius and height of a closed cylinder of volume 330 cm^3 with minimum surface area, compare it with a can I measured, and then improve the model until it explains the difference.

Measurements: Using a vernier caliper I measured my can's radius as 3.30 cm. Its full height is 11.5 cm, but that includes the narrowed neck, domed base and air space, so for a fair comparison I use an ideal cylinder of r = 3.30 cm holding exactly 330 cm^3: h = 330/(pi x 3.30^2) = 9.65 cm, so height/diameter = 9.65/6.60 = 1.46.

Model 1, least surface area: Let r be the radius and h the height in cm, and S the surface area in cm^2. The volume gives pi r^2 h = 330, so h = 330/(pi r^2). Substituting into S = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h gives S(r) = 2 pi r^2 + 660/r, for r > 0.
S'(r) = 4 pi r - 660/r^2. Setting S'(r) = 0: 4 pi r^3 = 660, r^3 = 165/pi, r = 3.745 cm. Then h = 330/(pi x 3.745^2) = 7.490 cm.
S''(r) = 4 pi + 1320/r^3, which is positive for every r > 0, so the curve is concave up everywhere and this stationary point is the global minimum, S = 264.4 cm^2. Figure 1 (S against r, plotted on my GDC) confirms one minimum at (3.745, 264.4).
I noticed h = 2r. This is not a coincidence: for any volume V, r^3 = V/(2 pi), so h = V/(pi r^2) = 2 pi r^3/(pi r^2) = 2r. The optimal can is always as tall as it is wide: height/diameter = 1.

Comparison: My can has ratio 1.46, not 1. Its area is S(3.30) = 2 pi (3.30)^2 + 660/3.30 = 268.4 cm^2, only 1.5% above the minimum. This surprised me: the curve is very flat near its minimum, so a large change in shape costs very little metal.

Model 2, wasted metal: Circular ends are stamped from sheet. If each circle is cut from a square of side 2r, the ends use 2(2r)^2 = 8r^2. M(r) = 8r^2 + 660/r, M'(r) = 16r - 660/r^2 = 0 gives r^3 = 41.25, r = 3.455 cm, h = 8.80 cm, and M''(r) = 16 + 1320/r^3 > 0 confirms a minimum. In general r^3 = V/8, so height/diameter = V/(2 pi r^3) = 4/pi = 1.27, again independent of V. This moves towards the real can but does not reach 1.46.

Model 3, thicker ends: The lid is noticeably thicker than the wall. Suppose each cm^2 of the ends costs k times as much as the wall. C(r) = 8k r^2 + 660/r, C'(r) = 16k r - 660/r^2 = 0, so r^3 = 330/(8k) and height/diameter = 4k/pi. For this to equal 1.46, k = 1.46 pi/4 = 1.15. The real shape is optimal if the ends cost about 15% more per unit area than the wall, which is believable.

Reflection: Each result holds only under its assumptions. Squares are a pessimistic cutting pattern; hexagonal packing wastes less, which lowers the ratio to about 1.10 and would need a larger k. I ignored the neck, the seam, and non-mathematical reasons such as fitting a hand or a fridge shelf, so k = 1.15 is a value that fits, not proof of the manufacturer's reasoning. A 0.01 cm error in my radius changes the ratio 1.46 by only about 0.01, so measurement is not the main weakness; the idealisation is. The most valuable thing I found was not h = 2r, which is well known, but the flatness of S near its minimum, because it explains why designers are free to choose a shape for other reasons.

Conclusion: The metal-minimising 330 cm^3 cylinder has r = 3.75 cm and h = 7.49 cm. Real cans are taller because end material is wasted and costs more, and because being away from the optimum costs only about 1.5%.

task: Mathematics exploration: What dimensions minimise the material used to make a 330 ml cylindrical drinks can, and why do real cans not have these dimensions?
text:
Introduction: I chose this topic because I drink a lot of soft drinks and I wanted to know if the cans are made in the best way. Companies want to save money so they should use the smallest amount of aluminium. My aim is to find the dimensions of a 330 ml can with the smallest surface area.

A can is a cylinder. The formulas are V = pi r^2 h and SA = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h.

Since the volume is 330, 330 = pi r^2 h so h = 330/(pi r^2). I put this into the surface area formula:
SA = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r (330/(pi r^2))
SA = 2 pi r^2 + 660/r

To find the minimum I differentiate and make it equal to zero.
dSA/dr = 4 pi r - 660/r^2
4 pi r - 660/r^2 = 0
4 pi r = 660/r^2
r^3 = 660/(4 pi) = 52.5
r = 3.74

Then h = 330/(pi x 3.74^2) = 7.51
SA = 2 pi (3.74)^2 + 660/3.74 = 264.4

So the best can has a radius of 3.74 and a height of 7.51. I also drew the graph on Desmos and it has a minimum point at the same place, which shows my answer is right.

Real can: I measured a real can and it has a radius of 3.3 cm and a height of 11.5 cm. This is different from my answer. The real can is taller and thinner than the best can. Its surface area is 2 pi (3.3)^2 + 2 pi (3.3)(11.5) = 306.9, which is more than 264.4. This means the company is using more aluminium than they need to. I think this could be because a tall can is easier to hold and looks better on the shelf.

Conclusion: In conclusion I found that the optimal can has r = 3.74 cm and h = 7.51 cm, and real cans are not optimal. I enjoyed this exploration and learned how calculus can be used in real life. If I had more time I would look at other shapes of can.

In conclusion maths is very useful in real life and I learned a lot about cylinders.

task: The number of fish in a lake t years after stocking is modelled by P(t) = 1200/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t)). (a) Find the initial population. (b) Find when the population reaches 900. (c) Show that the population grows fastest when P = 600 and find when this happens. (d) Interpret the long-term behaviour of the model and state one limitation.
text:
(a) At t = 0, e^0 = 1, so P(0) = 1200/(1 + 5) = 200. The lake was stocked with 200 fish.

(b) Set P = 900: 1200/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t)) = 900
1 + 5e^(-0.4t) = 1200/900 = 4/3
5e^(-0.4t) = 1/3
e^(-0.4t) = 1/15
-0.4t = ln(1/15) = -ln 15
t = ln 15/0.4 = 6.77 (3 s.f.)
The population reaches 900 after about 6.8 years. Check: P(6.77) = 1200/(1 + 5 x 0.0667) = 900.

(c) Let u = e^(-0.4t), so P = 1200(1 + 5u)^-1 and du/dt = -0.4u.
By the chain rule, dP/dt = -1200(1 + 5u)^-2 x 5 x (-0.4u) = 2400u/(1 + 5u)^2.
To write this in terms of P: P/1200 = 1/(1 + 5u), so 1 - P/1200 = 5u/(1 + 5u).
Then 0.4P(1 - P/1200) = 0.4 x 1200/(1 + 5u) x 5u/(1 + 5u) = 2400u/(1 + 5u)^2 = dP/dt.
So the growth rate is G(P) = 0.4P - P^2/3000, a quadratic in P with negative leading coefficient, so its vertex is a maximum. dG/dP = 0.4 - P/1500 = 0 gives P = 600. Since P increases continuously from 200 towards 1200 it passes through 600 exactly once, so the growth rate is greatest when P = 600, as required.
Time: 1200/(1 + 5u) = 600 gives 1 + 5u = 2, u = 1/5, -0.4t = -ln 5, t = ln 5/0.4 = 4.02 years (3 s.f.). The maximum rate is G(600) = 0.4 x 600 x 0.5 = 120 fish per year.

(d) As t tends to infinity, e^(-0.4t) tends to 0, so P tends to 1200/1 = 1200, and P is always below 1200 because 5e^(-0.4t) > 0. In context 1200 is the carrying capacity of the lake: the population rises quickly at first, fastest at half the capacity after about 4 years, then levels off as food and space limit growth. Limitation: the model assumes conditions in the lake never change, so the capacity stays at 1200 and the growth constant at 0.4. It ignores fishing, disease and seasonal breeding, and it gives non-integer numbers of fish, so it is only an approximation.

task: The number of fish in a lake t years after stocking is modelled by P(t) = 1200/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t)). (a) Find the initial population. (b) Find when the population reaches 900. (c) Show that the population grows fastest when P = 600 and find when this happens. (d) Interpret the long-term behaviour of the model and state one limitation.
text:
(a) P(0) = 1200/(1 + 5e^0) = 1200/6 = 200

(b) 900 = 1200/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t))
1 + 5e^(-0.4t) = 1.333
5e^(-0.4t) = 0.333
e^(-0.4t) = 0.0667
-0.4t = ln(0.0667) = -2.708
t = 6.77

(c) dP/dt = 1200 x 5 x 0.4e^(-0.4t)/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t))^2 = 2400e^(-0.4t)/(1 + 5e^(-0.4t))^2
I graphed dP/dt on my GDC and the maximum is at t = 4.02. Then P(4.02) = 599.6 which is about 600, so the population grows fastest when P = 600.

(d) When t gets very big the population goes to 1200, so there will be 1200 fish in the lake. A limitation is that the model might not be accurate in real life because it is only a model.

task: Visual Arts process portfolio: investigate how two artists represent home and memory, and show how this investigation developed your own ideas and skills.
text:
Investigation: Rachel Whiteread and Do Ho Suh

My starting point was my grandmother's flat, which was sold this year. I wanted to find artists who make a home visible after it has gone, so I compared Rachel Whiteread's 'House' (1993) with Do Ho Suh's 'Seoul Home/L.A. Home' (1999).

Whiteread cast the whole interior of a condemned Victorian terraced house in east London in concrete and then removed the walls. What is left is the air of the rooms made solid: fireplaces bulge outwards, window recesses become blocks, the door is sealed. Studying photographs, I noticed the surface carries a negative imprint of every skirting board and socket, so the work is extremely specific, yet nobody can enter it. I read this as memory that is complete but closed. The context matters: the street was being cleared, and the sculpture itself was demolished in early 1994, so the work argued about housing and loss in public and was fought over in public. Its weight, greyness and blankness bring it closer to a tomb or war memorial than to a house.

Suh does the opposite with the same subject. He measured his parents' traditional Korean house and remade it in translucent celadon-green silk, sewn with every lintel and lattice, and hung it from the ceiling. It folds into a suitcase, and the title grows with the name of each city where it is shown. Where Whiteread's home is fixed to its site, Suh's is all movement: it comes from leaving Seoul for the United States, and he has spoken of wanting to carry his home with him. The fabric is one used for traditional Korean summer clothing, so the material is a cultural memory too. Viewers walk underneath and see through it, so the memory is open but weightless, almost not there.

Comparing them changed my question from how do I show the flat to whether my memory of it is heavy or light. I decided it is both: the objects are heavy, the rooms are already fading.

Developing ideas and skills: I tested both languages. Experiment 1 was a plaster cast of the inside of her sewing drawer. The first cast broke because I had not sealed the wood and the plaster gripped the grain; for the second I used two coats of petroleum jelly and a hessian layer for strength, and it released cleanly, showing the dovetail joints in negative. It was convincing but felt borrowed from Whiteread, and too funereal for a woman who was always sewing. Experiment 2 followed Suh's later rubbing works: I laid tracing paper over her front door and rubbed it with graphite. A soft 6B filled the grain and lost detail; a harder 2B stick used on its side picked up the letterbox and the scratches around the lock. Experiment 3 combined them: I machine-stitched the outline of the door panels into white organza, using the rubbing as a pattern. Puckering was a problem until I used a water-soluble stabiliser and lowered the thread tension.

When I reviewed the three with my class, people touched the organza and ignored the plaster, which confirmed what the comparison suggested: lightness invites the viewer in. My resolved idea is a full-size organza door, hung so that it moves, with the plaster drawer on the floor beneath it as the single heavy thing, so that Whiteread's weight and Suh's transparency are both present, but in my own proportion.

task: Visual Arts process portfolio: investigate how two artists represent home and memory, and show how this investigation developed your own ideas and skills.
text:
Artist research: Rachel Whiteread and Do Ho Suh

For my theme of home I researched two artists. Rachel Whiteread is a British artist born in 1963. She was the first woman to win the Turner Prize, in 1993. Her most famous work is 'House', which was a concrete cast of the inside of a house in London. It was very big and grey and it was later knocked down. She also makes casts of smaller things like baths and the spaces under chairs. I think her work is about memory because the house is not there any more but you can still see its shape.

Do Ho Suh is a Korean artist born in 1962 who lives in London. He makes houses out of fabric. 'Seoul Home' is a copy of his childhood home made from green silk which hangs from the ceiling. It is see-through and very detailed. His work is about moving between different countries and missing home.

The two artists are similar because they both make work about houses, but they are different because Whiteread uses concrete, which is heavy, and Suh uses fabric, which is light. I prefer Do Ho Suh because his work is more colourful and delicate.

My own work: I was inspired by these artists to make work about my grandmother's flat. First I made a plaster cast of a drawer like Rachel Whiteread. The first one broke when I took it out, so I did it again and it worked better. Then I did some rubbings of her front door with pencil on tracing paper, like Do Ho Suh's rubbings. I also tried sewing on organza fabric, which was difficult because the fabric kept bunching up. I think the organza was the most successful experiment, so I will use it for my final piece, which will be a door made of fabric.

task: Visual Arts: write a reflection and evaluation of your final exhibition, covering your intentions, how the audience responded, the strengths and weaknesses of the work, and how it developed.
text:
Evaluation of my exhibition, 'Threshold'

Intentions: I set out to make a viewer feel what it is like to remember a home that no longer belongs to you: present in detail but impossible to enter. The exhibition has three pieces arranged as a short walk: a full-size door stitched in white organza, hung 20 cm from the wall; a plaster cast of the inside of my grandmother's sewing drawer on the floor beneath it; and six graphite rubbings of her door furniture on the facing wall.

How far the work meets them: The door is the strongest piece. Because it is lit from the side, the stitched panels throw a second, sharper door onto the wall, and when someone walks past the fabric moves while the shadow lags behind. I did not plan this; I found it when testing lights, and I kept the 20 cm gap because of it. It expresses the idea better than my original plan of a door hanging free in the middle of the room, since the viewer now sees a real thing and its memory at once. The plaster drawer works as a contrast in weight, and its position makes people look down and then up, which slows them.

The rubbings are the weakest part. They were process work that I promoted to finished pieces late, and it shows: they are on different papers, two are creased, and framed in a row they read as documents rather than as part of the walk. In hindsight four would have been stronger than six, or one large rubbing of the whole door at the same scale as the organza.

Audience: I watched visitors at the opening and left a comment book. Most went to the door first and several reached out to touch it, which tells me the lightness is inviting, as I hoped. However, three comments described the show as 'peaceful' or 'pretty', and only people who had read my text mentioned loss. So the work communicates fragility clearly but not absence; without the text it could be about any door. A younger student asked whose door it was, which made me realise that nothing in the room is specific to my grandmother except the drawer, and its meaning is hidden because it is a negative.

Development: The largest change over the project was moving from imitating Whiteread's casting to finding my own balance of heavy and light. Technically my stitching improved a great deal: the early samples pucker, and the final door only does so at the top hinge, where I rushed. I am less satisfied with how I managed time; leaving the rubbings to the last week is the direct cause of the weakest wall.

Next steps: To address the missing sense of loss I would add one trace of use, for example stitching the worn patch around the lock in a different thread, and I would replace the row of frames with a single door-sized rubbing. I would keep the lighting exactly as it is.

task: Visual Arts: write a reflection and evaluation of your final exhibition, covering your intentions, how the audience responded, the strengths and weaknesses of the work, and how it developed.
text:
Evaluation of my exhibition

My exhibition is called 'Threshold' and it is about my grandmother's flat and my memories of it. I wanted to show how memories of a home can fade. There are three pieces: a door made from organza fabric, a plaster cast of a drawer, and six rubbings of the door handle and letterbox.

I think the exhibition was successful overall. The organza door is my favourite piece because it took the longest and the stitching is neat. It looks good with the light shining on it and makes a shadow on the wall. The plaster drawer also came out well and shows my casting skills. The rubbings are less successful because some of them got creased and they are on different paper.

At the opening people said they liked my work. Lots of people said the door was beautiful and one person said it was peaceful. This shows that the audience understood my work.

During the project I improved my sewing skills a lot and I learned how to cast with plaster. At the beginning my stitching was messy but by the end it was much better. If I did the project again I would manage my time better and I would redo the rubbings more carefully. I would also add more pieces so the exhibition filled the space.

task: Visual Arts: write a reflection and evaluation of your final exhibition, covering your intentions, how the audience responded, the strengths and weaknesses of the work, and how it developed.
text: My exhibition is about my grandmother's flat. I made a door out of fabric, a plaster drawer and some rubbings. I am happy with how it turned out and I think it looks good. Everyone who came said they liked it. The door was the hardest to make and took a long time. I worked hard on this project and I am proud of it. If I did it again I would not change anything except maybe start earlier.
